newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Analysts say Clariant gains from Hoechst.
newsitem.headline: Analysts say Clariant gains from Hoechst.

text.p: Swiss specialty chemicals group Clariant AG made a good deal by agreeing to merge with the related business of German giant Hoechst AG, analysts said.
Analysts noted there was little information on the details of the deal in an identical media statement released by both companies.

But they approved of the choice of a merger rather than a potentially more expensive acquisition, which would have been the other choice as Clariant sought to grow fast after being split off from Sandoz AG last year.
"This is shareholder friendly because it avoids dilution and the higher costs of an acquisition," said Claudio Werder of Bank Vontobel.
Werder said the deal appeared to be good for Clariant by strengthening and rounding out its market positions.
Michael Sjoestrom from Geneva private bankers Pictet & Cie said the deal would help Clariant overcome two key obstacles.
"Clariant had two problems: it needed critical mass, and it needed to reduce an overwhelming dependency on textile dyes, which is a dwindling market," Sjoestrom told Reuters.
"This deal moves Clariant towards critical mass and reduces the impact on the bottom-line of the textile dyes business," Sjoestrom said.

Sjoestrom also said the pact seemed to be friendly to Clariant shareholders by trading less than half of Clariant capital for Hoechst business that will nearly quadruple the new group's annual sales to around eight billion Swiss francs from 2.3 billion now.

Beat Alpiger from Bank Baer said both companies were getting something in a mutually beneficial trade -- Hoechst getting rid of a sluggish business area and Clariant gaining size before bigger rival Ciba Speciality Chemicals is spun-off sometime next year.
An industry official close to the deal said both Clariant and Hoechst had carried out comprehensive restructuring in recent years.
By eliminating overlapping businesses after the merger, they will be able to further boost profitablity.
"Savings of several hundreds of millions of Swiss francs over a certain period of time should total about half a billion Swiss francs," the official, who declined to be named, told Reuters.
